summary: Describes the Telephony Gateway Registration Protocol, used to register telephone prefixes handled by gateways and soft switches. It can also export resource information to a TRIP Location Server. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Phone gateways use it to tell a central directory which phone number ranges they can handle.

how do gateways register with a location server
subtitle: How phone gateways tell a signaling server which numbers and trunks they can reach, and how many circuits are free.

tldr.problem: A VoIP domain runs many gateways to the telephone network, and its proxy needs real-time information such as remaining capacity to pick one for each call. TRIP carries routes between providers but does not say how routes get injected from inside the network or how a specific gateway is chosen.
tldr.mechanism: TGREP reuses TRIP's message formats and session procedures, with the gateway as a send-only peer. It adds new attributes (circuit capacity, available circuits, call success, prefixes, trunk groups, carriers) and two new address families.
tldr.outcome: A receiver in front of the gateways can consolidate and aggregate the routes, then hand them to a TRIP Location Server. It is a Proposed Standard with no replacement listed.

today: RFC 5140 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds directly on RFC 3219 (TRIP).

sections.title: The Gateway Registration Problem
sections.content:
An Internet Telephony Administrative Domain (ITAD) typically deploys many gateways for geographic diversity, capacity and redundancy. It often splits its network into Points of Presence (POPs), each with some gateways and a proxy element (a SIP proxy or H.323 gatekeeper) in front of them. The proxy decides which gateway receives each arriving call.

That choice depends on availability, remaining call capacity and call success statistics toward a given PSTN destination, so the proxy needs this information in real time. TRIP (RFC 3219) carries telephony routes between providers, but it has no mechanism for injecting routes from inside the network or for selecting the specific terminating gateway. TGREP fills those gaps.

TGREP is identical to TRIP in syntax and overall operation. It differs in the route processing rules of the receiver, which allow consolidation, and it defines new attributes. It uses only a subset of TRIP, and its two ends are asymmetric, whereas TRIP allows symmetric and asymmetric peers.
sections.eli5: A phone company has many exits to the regular phone network and needs to know which exit is free before it sends a call. TGREP is the way the exits report in.

sections.title: Senders, Receivers and Location Servers
sections.content:
The TGREP sender lives on the gateway and gathers its information. The TGREP receiver (also called the Ingress LS) peers with one or more gateways, optionally consolidates and aggregates what it hears, and hands the result to the Egress LS, a TRIP Location Server that disseminates routes over TRIP. The routing proxy also uses the information to choose a gateway. The interface between the Ingress LS and the Egress LS is a local matter.

The sender opens a session with a procedure similar to TRIP session establishment, then sends reachability information in UPDATE messages that have the same format as in TRIP. Seven TRIP attributes do not apply and a receiver MAY ignore them: AdvertisementPath, RoutedPath, AtomicAggregate, LocalPreference, MultiExitDisc, ITADTopology and ConvertedRoute.
sections.eli5: Each gateway has a messenger that reports to a collector. The collector tidies up all the reports and passes them on to the office that talks to the outside world.

sections.title: TGREP Attributes
sections.content:
From TRIP, TGREP uses WithdrawnRoutes, ReachableRoutes, NexthopServer, Prefix and Communities. It adds new attributes, all non-mandatory and not well-known:

  • TotalCircuitCapacity (type 13): a 4-octet unsigned integer for the provisioned number of circuits. It changes rarely, so the LS MAY propagate it, and aggregated routes SHOULD sum the values.
  • AvailableCircuits (type 14): a 4-octet unsigned integer for the circuits currently free. It is used only between a gateway and its managing LS, and routes MUST NOT be disseminated with it.
  • CallSuccess (type 15): two 4-octet unsigned integers, the calls terminated successfully and the calls attempted over the same window of time. It is also used only between gateway and LS and MUST NOT be disseminated. The gateway decides how disconnect causes map to success.
  • Prefix (types 16, 17 and 18 for E.164, Pentadecimal and Decimal routing numbers): a list of prefixes, each with a 2-octet length. A zero-length attribute means the gateway can terminate all prefixes of that type, which is not the same as omitting the attribute.
  • TrunkGroup (type 19) and Carrier (type 20): lists of identifiers, each with a 1-octet length. A trunk group value is a label and a trunk context separated by a semicolon. A zero-length attribute means all trunk groups or all carriers.

Routes with differing Prefix, TrunkGroup or Carrier attributes MUST NOT be aggregated. TrunkGroup SHOULD NOT be disseminated outside the ITAD.
sections.eli5: Each report can include extra notes: how many phone lines exist, how many are free, how many calls worked, and which numbers, line bundles or phone companies the door leads to.

sections.title: TrunkGroup and Carrier Address Families
sections.content:
TGREP defines two new TRIP address families: 4 for TrunkGroup and 5 for Carrier. They are flat, not hierarchical. They let a gateway attach properties such as AvailableCircuits to a trunk group or carrier rather than to a prefix, so a service provider can route strictly by trunk group or carrier.

The RFC gives scalability as a benefit: gateways can have hundreds or a few thousand circuits, and reporting at trunk group or carrier granularity can reduce UPDATE traffic. A gateway that supports these families should list them as route types in the OPEN message capability negotiation.

AvailableCircuits, TotalCircuitCapacity and CallSuccess work with all address families, and are recommended with TrunkGroup or Carrier. The Prefix attribute cannot be used with the E.164, Pentadecimal or Decimal families. The Carrier attribute cannot be used with the Carrier family, and TrunkGroup cannot be used with the TrunkGroup family.
sections.eli5: Instead of reporting for every phone number, a gateway can report for a whole bundle of lines or for a whole phone company. That means fewer, simpler reports.

sections.title: Gateway Operation
sections.content:
The gateway operates in TRIP Send Only mode: it advertises its own reachability and does not learn about others. It sends an OPEN message with the Send Receive Capability set to Send Only, listing its supported address families, and the rest of session setup is identical to TRIP. It then sends UPDATE messages with its entire reachability and attributes. KEEPALIVE messages follow TRIP.

Error handling follows TRIP with one difference: a gateway never sends a NOTIFICATION in response to an UPDATE, and any UPDATE it receives is silently discarded. In the Established state it stays Established. Otherwise the TGREP and TRIP state machines are identical.

A gateway keeps one call routing database per peer LS (called Adj-TRIBs-GW-Out) and has no equivalents of Adj-TRIBs-In or Loc-TRIB. It MUST NOT implement TRIP route selection and aggregation.

A single session MUST NOT send UPDATEs for more than one of these categories: prefix families (E.164, Pentadecimal, Decimal), TrunkGroup, or Carrier. An OPEN that violates this should be rejected with a NOTIFICATION.
sections.eli5: The gateway only talks and never listens for routes. If anyone sends it routes anyway, it quietly ignores them. Each conversation is about one kind of thing, not a mix.

sections.title: Consolidation and Aggregation
sections.content:
The receiver applies consolidation first and aggregation second. Consolidation (RECOMMENDED) combines multiple routes for the same destination, possibly from different gateways, so routing information is not lost. If gateway A advertises destination SIP 408 with Carrier C1 and gateway B advertises it with Carrier C2, the consolidated route carries both, C1 C2. Prefix values {408, 650} and {919, 973} from two Carrier updates can become {408, 650, 919, 973}. The details are left to each implementation.

Aggregation combines routes for different destinations into a summary, following TRIP's procedures and each attribute's aggregation rules. For example, routes for 4080 through 4089 could be summarized as 408.
sections.eli5: If two doors both lead to room 408 through different hallways, the collector writes one note listing both hallways. That is consolidation. Squashing the notes for rooms 4080 to 4089 into one note for the 408 wing is aggregation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations are identical to those of TRIP and are restated. The mechanism for the session between a TGREP gateway and a TRIP LS in an IP network is IPsec, using the Authentication Header (AH) or Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

AH gives data origin authentication, connectionless integrity and optional anti-replay protection. ESP adds confidentiality. Implementations using ESP SHALL comply with section 3.1.1 of RFC 4835, and those using AH with section 3.2. Implementations SHOULD use IKEv2 and, when they do, SHOULD support 3DES-CBC for confidentiality and HMAC-SHA1 for integrity.
sections.eli5: The reports travel in a locked, signed envelope so nobody can read them or swap them on the way.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: TRIP and TGREP share the same IANA registries for capabilities, attributes, address families and application protocols. IANA added attribute codes 13 through 20 (TotalCircuitCapacity, AvailableCircuits, CallSuccess, the three Prefix types, TrunkGroup and Carrier), address family code 4 (TrunkGroup) and code 5 (Carrier).
sections.eli5: The official list of codes got eight new attribute numbers and two new kinds of address, so everyone uses the same ones.
